terms.tooltip: Estimated chance this stock beats its benchmark over the stated horizon.
terms.plain_meaning: A single percent that answers one question: over the next year (or chosen window), how likely is this company to do better than a benchmark like the S&P 500? A 61% means the model estimates a bit better than even odds of beating it.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the one honest number the whole app is built around, and it is calibrated so a stated percent means what it says.
terms.fincompass_use: This is the Forecast itself — the headline percent shown identically on the Guided and Research screens. The interpretation policy sits on top of it but never changes it.
terms.limitation: It is not a target price, an expected return, an accuracy figure, or advice. A 61% guess can still be wrong on this name and date.
terms.technical_definition: A calibrated estimate P(asset return > benchmark return) over a fixed horizon, conditioned on the model's information set at the training cutoff.

terms.tooltip: How much a forecast has been validated: Limited, Research, or Market.
terms.plain_meaning: A label saying how much testing stands behind a forecast. Limited means the number is coherent but not proven skillful; Research means it passed locked tests on a defined dataset; Market means it also passed stronger, point-in-time controls on a broader universe.
terms.why_it_matters: The same percent means different things depending on how much validation backs it, so the tier tells you how much weight to give it.
terms.fincompass_use: Shown as a plain label next to every Forecast and used by the interpretation policy: a Limited-evidence forecast can only ever justify Watch, never a money action.
terms.limitation: A high tier means the machinery was validated, not that this specific future is predictable; validity is not the same as strong skill.
terms.technical_definition: An ordinal validation rank — Limited (Bayesian baseline), Research validated, Market validated — with an Invalid state below all three.

terms.tooltip: The asset types and regions a model is allowed to forecast.
terms.plain_meaning: The boundary of what a model is qualified to score. A model trained on US stocks should not hand you a forecast for a foreign bond or a crypto token — that falls outside its domain.
terms.why_it_matters: A model asked to forecast something it never learned will produce a confident but meaningless number, so the domain guards against that.
terms.fincompass_use: Enforced before a Forecast is produced: if a ticker falls outside the model's domain, FinCompass declines to forecast (analytics may still run).
terms.limitation: Being inside the domain does not guarantee accuracy; it only rules out obviously unsupported cases.
terms.technical_definition: The declared region of feature/instrument space (asset class, region, liquidity) over which a model's validation is considered to hold.

terms.tooltip: A model trained across many names rather than one single stock.
terms.plain_meaning: Instead of fitting a separate model to each company, a pooled model learns from many companies at once and applies the shared pattern to each one. This gives more data to learn from when any single name has a short history.
terms.why_it_matters: Single-name histories are short and noisy; pooling borrows strength across names to make estimates steadier.
terms.fincompass_use: The shipped US artifacts are pooled models (Bayesian baselines and a research-validated ensemble) applied to individual tickers within their domain.
terms.limitation: Pooling assumes names are similar enough to share a pattern; a company that behaves unlike the pool can be mis-forecast.
terms.technical_definition: A model estimated on a cross-section of instruments with shared parameters, optionally with partial pooling toward per-instrument effects.

terms.tooltip: The date after which no data was used to fit the model.
terms.plain_meaning: The line in time where the model stopped learning. Everything before it could be used to train; nothing after it was seen. This keeps the model from cheating by peeking at the future.
terms.why_it_matters: Honest forecasting requires that the model never saw the outcome it is being tested on, and the cutoff makes that boundary explicit.
terms.fincompass_use: Recorded in each model's manifest and shown on the Research screen; also drives the model-training-freshness concept.
terms.limitation: A recent cutoff does not make a model good — it only means the data is not stale; the fit could still be weak.
terms.technical_definition: The timestamp separating in-sample data (used for fitting) from out-of-sample data, enforcing chronological validity.

terms.tooltip: How much better the model's probabilities score than a naive baseline.
terms.plain_meaning: A grade for probability forecasts. The Brier score measures how far the forecasts were from what actually happened; Brier skill compares that to a simple baseline, so positive means the model beat guessing and higher is better.
terms.why_it_matters: It rewards being both accurate and honestly calibrated, penalizing overconfident wrong calls.
terms.fincompass_use: One of the scoring rules reported on the Research screen and used in validation gates for the Research and Market tiers.
terms.limitation: A single skill number hides where the model fails; it can look fine overall while being poor in a specific regime.
terms.technical_definition: Brier skill score = 1 − (BS_model / BS_reference), where BS = mean((p − outcome)^2) and outcome ∈ {0,1}.

terms.tooltip: Skill measured by log-loss: how well probabilities matched outcomes.
terms.plain_meaning: Another grade for probability forecasts that punishes confident mistakes very hard. Log-loss skill compares the model's log-loss to a baseline, so positive means it beat the baseline.
terms.why_it_matters: Because it heavily penalizes being confidently wrong, it is a strict test of honest probabilities.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported alongside Brier skill on the Research screen as a second scoring rule for the forecast.
terms.limitation: It can be dominated by a few extreme misses and is undefined for probabilities of exactly 0 or 1.
terms.technical_definition: 1 − (LL_model / LL_reference) where LL = −mean(y·log p + (1−y)·log(1−p)).

terms.tooltip: Chance the model ranks a true winner above a true loser.
terms.plain_meaning: A measure of how well the model separates winners from losers. 0.5 is coin-flip ranking; 1.0 is perfect. It asks: pick a real outperformer and a real underperformer at random — how often does the model score the winner higher?
terms.why_it_matters: It captures ranking ability independent of the exact probability level, which matters when you compare names.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported on the Research screen as a discrimination metric for the forecast model.
terms.limitation: It says nothing about calibration — a model can rank perfectly yet still output badly miscalibrated percents.
terms.technical_definition: Area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve; equals P(score of a positive > score of a negative).

terms.tooltip: Gap between predicted percents and how often they actually happen.
terms.plain_meaning: A check on whether the percents are truthful. Of all the times the model said 60%, did the event happen about 60% of the time? Expected Calibration Error averages that gap across probability bins — smaller is better.
terms.why_it_matters: Calibration is what lets you read a FinCompass percent literally rather than as a vague confidence.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported (ECE) on the Research screen and used as a validation gate; good calibration is central to the product's promise.
terms.limitation: Low ECE across all names does not guarantee calibration within a subgroup, and it depends on how bins are chosen.
terms.technical_definition: Expected Calibration Error = weighted mean over bins of |average predicted probability − observed frequency|.

terms.tooltip: Whether the model is over- or under-confident overall.
terms.plain_meaning: A single number describing the tilt of the calibration line. A slope of 1 is ideal; below 1 means the model is overconfident (its extremes are too extreme), above 1 means underconfident.
terms.why_it_matters: It summarizes the direction of miscalibration, which tells you whether to trust the model's strong calls.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported on the Research screen as a complement to ECE for judging calibration quality.
terms.limitation: A slope near 1 can still hide local wiggles; it is a global summary, not a full picture.
terms.technical_definition: Slope of a logistic regression of outcomes on the logit of predicted probabilities; ideal value is 1.

terms.tooltip: Updated belief about an unknown after combining prior and data.
terms.plain_meaning: A way of stating what you believe after weighing evidence. You start with a prior belief, observe data, and end with a posterior belief. The posterior is a full distribution, not just one number, so it carries its own uncertainty.
terms.why_it_matters: It produces honest probabilities that widen when data is thin instead of pretending to precision.
terms.fincompass_use: The Limited-evidence (baseline) Forecasts are Bayesian: a coherent posterior probability of outperformance when stronger skill has not been demonstrated.
terms.limitation: A coherent posterior is only as good as its prior and model; coherent does not mean skillful, which is why it stays Limited-evidence.
terms.technical_definition: posterior(θ|data) ∝ likelihood(data|θ) × prior(θ), by Bayes' theorem.

terms.tooltip: Declared rules that turn a probability into a plain posture, without changing it.
terms.plain_meaning: A fixed, published set of rules that reads a forecast and suggests a plain posture — Don't decide, Watch, DCA a little, Hold, or Trim. It sits on top of the number and never edits the number itself.
terms.why_it_matters: It keeps the honest probability separate from any practical suggestion, so validation and interpretation never get confused.
terms.fincompass_use: Implemented as action_policy_v1: thresholds (e.g. 0.58 / 0.42) are declared, separately versioned policy assumptions, not statistical results. Limited evidence can only yield Watch.
terms.limitation: It does not account for your taxes, costs, risk tolerance, or portfolio, and it is explicitly not advice or model validation.
terms.technical_definition: A versioned deterministic mapping from (probability, evidence tier, data status, safety flag, position weight) to one of five postures.

terms.tooltip: The rules controlling how models are validated, versioned, and allowed to act.
terms.plain_meaning: The guardrails around the models: what tier a model earns, where it is allowed to forecast, what it may do in Live, and how any change is versioned rather than silently tweaked.
terms.why_it_matters: It stops a weak or misapplied model from being trusted like a strong one and keeps changes auditable.
terms.fincompass_use: Expressed through evidence tiers, applicability domains, the frozen interpretation policy, and manifests; a Limited model is tracking-only in Live.
terms.limitation: Governance constrains misuse but cannot make an unpredictable target predictable.
terms.technical_definition: The set of versioned constraints and manifests binding a model's validation status to its permitted forecasting and Live behavior.

terms.tooltip: Non-negotiable checks a model must pass to forecast at all.
terms.plain_meaning: The pass/fail gate before any skill is even considered: correct chronology (no peeking at the future), a real fit, sound features, and an in-domain request. Fail any and the model is Invalid and produces no forecast.
terms.why_it_matters: It rules out forecasts that are broken by construction, before anyone looks at how skillful they seem.
terms.fincompass_use: Enforced ahead of tier assignment; an Invalid model cannot Forecast or run Live at all.
terms.limitation: Passing hard validity only means the model is not broken — it says nothing about how good the forecast is.
terms.technical_definition: A conjunction of gating checks (chronology, fit, feature integrity, applicability) that must all pass for a model to be usable.

terms.tooltip: Live watches the frozen forecast but never adjusts it.
terms.plain_meaning: A Live mode that observes how a forecast plays out over time but does not change the number. It records outcomes and displays them without touching the frozen probability.
terms.why_it_matters: It lets a weakly validated model be monitored honestly without letting it adapt on evidence it has not earned.
terms.fincompass_use: The mandatory Live mode for Limited-evidence (Bayesian baseline) models — they can only track, never adapt.
terms.limitation: It gives no updated probability; if conditions change, the frozen forecast stays put until you re-forecast.
terms.technical_definition: A Live configuration that logs realized outcomes against a frozen forecast with zero residual applied.

terms.tooltip: Live may apply a small, gated residual after outcomes mature.
terms.plain_meaning: A Live mode where the app may nudge the forecast by a small, controlled amount — but only after real outcomes have come in and passed a quality gate. The base forecast stays frozen; the nudge is a bounded residual on top.
terms.why_it_matters: It lets a stronger model react to fresh evidence without abandoning the validated forecast it started from.
terms.fincompass_use: Available only to Research- and Market-validated models, and only through a gated residual that waits for delayed labels to mature.
terms.limitation: The residual can stay frozen for a long time when labels have not matured, so 'adaptive' does not mean 'reacts quickly'.
terms.technical_definition: A Live configuration applying a bounded, gate-controlled residual to a frozen forecast once matured outcomes justify it.

terms.tooltip: Predict first, then learn from the outcome, in sequence.
terms.plain_meaning: A test-then-learn discipline: the model makes each forecast before seeing the result, then updates only after the true outcome arrives. Every update is judged on data the model had not yet seen.
terms.why_it_matters: It keeps online learning honest, because the model is always scored on genuine out-of-sample predictions.
terms.fincompass_use: The principle behind adaptive Live: forecasts are made, outcomes observed, and only then can a gated residual update.
terms.limitation: It is slow when outcomes take a year to mature, so honest updates can be infrequent.
terms.technical_definition: Sequential predict-then-update evaluation where each prediction is scored before its outcome is used for learning.

terms.tooltip: Outcomes that only become known long after the forecast is made.
terms.plain_meaning: The true answer to a 12-month forecast is not known for 12 months. Until then the outcome (label) is pending, so the model cannot yet learn from that case.
terms.why_it_matters: It explains why adaptive Live can sit frozen for months — it is correctly waiting for outcomes to mature.
terms.fincompass_use: Tracked as pending labels in the realtime layer; the Live gate only acts once labels have matured.
terms.limitation: Because labels overlap in time, the number of matured outcomes is far smaller than the number of forecasts made.
terms.technical_definition: Target outcomes that resolve only after a fixed horizon, creating a lag between prediction and supervised feedback.

terms.tooltip: Whether and how a model can be refit as new data arrives.
terms.plain_meaning: How readily a model can be rebuilt on newer data. Some models can be periodically retrained as fresh, matured outcomes accumulate; others are frozen artifacts you must rebuild deliberately.
terms.why_it_matters: It sets expectations for how a forecast keeps pace with a changing world versus needing a manual rebuild.
terms.fincompass_use: Reflected in the model ladder and Live behavior; retraining respects chronology and the same validation gates as the original fit.
terms.limitation: Frequent retraining risks overfitting to noise and can quietly change behavior if not re-validated and re-versioned.
terms.technical_definition: The capacity to refit a model on an extended, chronologically valid dataset under the same validation protocol.

terms.tooltip: How recent the price/fundamental data for this ticker is.
terms.plain_meaning: How up to date the raw inputs for a specific stock are — the latest price and fundamentals FinCompass has for that name. Stale inputs can make any calculation lag reality.
terms.why_it_matters: Analytics and forecasts are only as current as the data feeding them, so knowing the data's age is essential.
terms.fincompass_use: One of three distinct freshness concepts FinCompass surfaces, describing the age of the instrument's own data.
terms.limitation: Fresh data does not mean correct data — free public prices can still be revised, late, or missing.
terms.technical_definition: The recency of the most recent observation in an instrument's local price/fundamental series.

terms.tooltip: How long ago the model itself was last trained.
terms.plain_meaning: How recently the model was fit, based on its training cutoff. A model trained years ago may not reflect newer market behavior even if today's price data is fresh.
terms.why_it_matters: An old model on fresh data can still be out of step, so its own age matters separately.
terms.fincompass_use: A second of the three freshness concepts, derived from each model's training cutoff and shown with the Forecast.
terms.limitation: A recently trained model is not automatically better; freshness is about age, not skill.
terms.technical_definition: Elapsed time since a model's training cutoff, indicating how current its learned parameters are.

terms.tooltip: A model inferring hidden market states like calm vs turbulent.
terms.plain_meaning: Markets seem to switch between hidden states — for example calm, trending, or turbulent. A Hidden Markov Model infers which state is likely active now from the data, without being told directly.
terms.why_it_matters: Behavior and risk differ sharply by regime, so knowing the likely state adds context to a forecast or risk figure.
terms.fincompass_use: Used as an analytics/context signal for market state; it is not a Forecast feature unless a versioned contract admits it.
terms.limitation: Regimes are inferred, not observed, and the model can label a state late or wrongly, especially at turning points.
terms.technical_definition: A Hidden Markov Model with latent discrete states and state-dependent emission distributions estimated from observed returns.

terms.tooltip: Average yearly growth rate implied by a period's total return.
terms.plain_meaning: Takes the total gain over some period and expresses it as an equivalent steady yearly rate, so you can compare investments held for different lengths of time on the same footing.
terms.why_it_matters: It normalizes returns to a per-year basis, making a 3-month result and a 5-year result comparable.
terms.fincompass_use: A deterministic output of the Performance analytics desk computed from the instrument's return history.
terms.limitation: It smooths over the path — two assets with the same annualized return can have wildly different bumps and drawdowns.
terms.technical_definition: Geometric mean growth rate: (ending/beginning)^(1/years) − 1, or (1 + total return)^(periods per year / periods) − 1.

terms.tooltip: How much returns swing around their average.
terms.plain_meaning: A measure of how bumpy an investment's returns are. High volatility means big ups and downs; low volatility means a smoother ride. It is usually quoted per year.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the most common quick gauge of risk and feeds many other measures like Sharpe.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Performance and Risk desks, typically annualized, as the standard deviation of returns.
terms.limitation: It treats upside and downside swings the same and assumes swings resemble the past, which fails in crises.
terms.technical_definition: Standard deviation of periodic returns, scaled to annual by multiplying by sqrt(periods per year).

terms.tooltip: Excess return earned per unit of total volatility.
terms.plain_meaning: Reward for the bumpiness you endured: it divides return above the risk-free rate by total volatility. Higher means more return per unit of risk taken.
terms.why_it_matters: It lets you compare investments on risk-adjusted terms rather than raw return alone.
terms.fincompass_use: A standard risk-adjusted metric in the Performance desk, computed from returns and a risk-free rate.
terms.limitation: It penalizes upside volatility as if it were risk and assumes roughly normal returns, understating tail risk.
terms.technical_definition: (mean portfolio return − risk-free rate) / standard deviation of portfolio returns.

terms.tooltip: Excess return per unit of downside-only volatility.
terms.plain_meaning: Like Sharpe, but it only counts the bad kind of volatility — the downside swings — as risk. Upside jumps are not held against the investment.
terms.why_it_matters: For most investors only downside hurts, so Sortino can be a fairer risk-adjusted score than Sharpe.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported by the Performance desk alongside Sharpe as a downside-focused risk-adjusted metric.
terms.limitation: It needs a chosen threshold and enough downside observations; with few losses the downside estimate is unstable.
terms.technical_definition: (mean return − target) / downside deviation, where downside deviation uses only returns below the target.

terms.tooltip: Worst peak-to-trough drop over the period.
terms.plain_meaning: The deepest fall from a high point to a later low before recovering. If an investment went from 100 to 60 before climbing back, its max drawdown was 40%.
terms.why_it_matters: It captures the worst pain an investor would have had to sit through, which drives real-world behavior.
terms.fincompass_use: A Performance-desk statistic computed from the cumulative return path.
terms.limitation: It reflects only the single worst episode in the sample and says nothing about how often such drops occur.
terms.technical_definition: Maximum of (peak value − trough value) / peak value over the observation window.

terms.tooltip: How much a stock moves with the overall market.
terms.plain_meaning: A sensitivity number: a beta of 1 moves with the market, 2 tends to move twice as much, and 0.5 half as much. It measures exposure to broad market swings.
terms.why_it_matters: It tells you how much of a stock's movement is just the market pulling it along.
terms.fincompass_use: Estimated by the Performance and Factors desks by regressing the asset's returns on the market's.
terms.limitation: Beta is backward-looking and unstable over time; it only captures the linear, market-wide part of risk.
terms.technical_definition: Slope of the regression of asset excess returns on market excess returns: Cov(R_a, R_m) / Var(R_m).

terms.tooltip: Return beyond what market exposure alone would explain.
terms.plain_meaning: The part of an investment's return that is not explained by simply riding the market. Positive alpha means it did better than its market exposure predicted.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the classic measure of skill or edge after accounting for market risk.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported by the Factors and Performance desks as the intercept of a returns regression.
terms.limitation: Estimated alpha is noisy and can vanish after costs; it depends entirely on the risk model chosen.
terms.technical_definition: Intercept α in R_a − R_f = α + β(R_m − R_f) + ε.
terms.formula: α = intercept of asset excess return on market excess return

terms.tooltip: Share of a variable's movement explained by the model.
terms.plain_meaning: A 0-to-100% score of how much of something's ups and downs a model accounts for. An R-squared of 0.8 means the model explains 80% of the variation, leaving 20% unexplained.
terms.why_it_matters: It tells you how much of a return is captured by the chosen factors versus left as noise or alpha.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported in the Factors/regression desk to show how well the factor model fits the asset's returns.
terms.limitation: A high R-squared does not mean the model is causally correct, and it always rises as you add factors.
terms.technical_definition: 1 − (residual sum of squares / total sum of squares) from the regression.

terms.tooltip: Explaining returns with common drivers like market, size, and value.
terms.plain_meaning: A method that splits an investment's returns into a few common drivers — the overall market, company size, value versus growth, and so on — to see which forces move it.
terms.why_it_matters: It reveals what an investment is really exposed to, separating broad bets from genuine skill.
terms.fincompass_use: The Factors analytics desk fits a multi-factor regression of the asset's returns and reports the loadings, alpha, and R-squared.
terms.limitation: Results depend on which factors and history you choose, and loadings drift over time.
terms.technical_definition: OLS regression R_a − R_f = α + Σ_k β_k F_k + ε over chosen factor return series F_k.
terms.formula: R_a − R_f = α + Σ β_k F_k + ε

terms.tooltip: A loss threshold rarely exceeded, read from past returns.
terms.plain_meaning: A worst-case-ish loss figure taken straight from history. A 5% one-day VaR of 3% means that on the worst days — about 1 in 20 — losses were at least 3%, based on the past sample.
terms.why_it_matters: It gives a simple, data-driven sense of how bad a normal-bad day can be.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Risk desk from the empirical distribution of historical returns.
terms.limitation: It only knows losses inside the sample and says nothing about how bad the rare worse days beyond the threshold get.
terms.technical_definition: The negative of the chosen lower quantile (e.g. 5th percentile) of the historical return distribution.

terms.tooltip: Average loss on the days that breach the VaR threshold.
terms.plain_meaning: Goes one step past VaR: instead of the threshold, it asks how bad losses are on average when that threshold is breached. It captures the depth of the bad tail, not just its edge.
terms.why_it_matters: It describes how severe the rare-but-brutal days are, which VaR alone hides.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported by the Risk desk alongside VaR as expected shortfall from the historical distribution.
terms.limitation: The deep tail has few observations, so the estimate is noisy and still assumes the future resembles the sample.
terms.technical_definition: Expected loss conditional on the loss exceeding VaR: E[loss | loss > VaR_α].

terms.tooltip: Volatility weighted toward recent returns.
terms.plain_meaning: A volatility estimate that pays more attention to recent days than to the distant past, so it reacts faster when markets get choppy. EWMA stands for exponentially weighted moving average.
terms.why_it_matters: It tracks changing risk more responsively than a plain long-window standard deviation.
terms.fincompass_use: Offered by the Risk desk as a recency-weighted alternative volatility estimate.
terms.limitation: Its responsiveness depends on a chosen decay factor and it can overreact to a single shock.
terms.technical_definition: σ²_t = λ·σ²_{t−1} + (1−λ)·r²_{t−1}, with decay λ in (0,1).

terms.tooltip: Profit earned per dollar of shareholder equity.
terms.plain_meaning: Return on equity shows how much profit a company squeezes out of the money shareholders have put in. A 15% ROE means it earned 15 cents of profit per dollar of equity.
terms.why_it_matters: It is a headline gauge of how efficiently a business uses owners' capital.
terms.fincompass_use: A ratio computed by the Statements & ratios desk from net income and shareholder equity.
terms.limitation: It can be inflated by heavy debt or buybacks that shrink equity, so a high ROE is not automatically healthy.
terms.technical_definition: Net income divided by average shareholders' equity.

terms.tooltip: After-tax operating profit per dollar of invested capital.
terms.plain_meaning: Return on invested capital measures profit generated per dollar of all the money the business uses — both debt and equity. It reflects how good the core operations are at creating value.
terms.why_it_matters: Comparing ROIC to the cost of capital shows whether a company actually creates or destroys value.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Statements & ratios desk from after-tax operating profit and invested capital.
terms.limitation: Definitions of invested capital vary, and accounting choices (leases, goodwill) can distort it.
terms.technical_definition: NOPAT (net operating profit after tax) divided by invested capital (debt + equity − cash).

terms.tooltip: How much debt a company uses per dollar of equity.
terms.plain_meaning: Compares what a company owes to what shareholders own. A ratio of 2 means twice as much debt as equity, signaling heavier reliance on borrowing.
terms.why_it_matters: More debt amplifies both gains and losses and raises the risk of trouble in a downturn.
terms.fincompass_use: A leverage ratio from the Statements & ratios desk computed from total debt and equity.
terms.limitation: The 'right' level depends heavily on the industry, so the number is only meaningful in context.
terms.technical_definition: Total debt divided by total shareholders' equity.

terms.tooltip: Free cash flow as a percentage of market value.
terms.plain_meaning: Shows how much actual cash a company generates relative to its price. A 5% FCF yield means it produces 5 cents of free cash per dollar of market value each year.
terms.why_it_matters: Cash is harder to fake than earnings, so this is a grounded gauge of value and cash generation.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Statements & ratios desk from free cash flow and market capitalization (or enterprise value).
terms.limitation: Free cash flow swings with capital spending cycles, so a single year can mislead.
terms.technical_definition: Free cash flow divided by market capitalization (or enterprise value).
terms.formula: FCF yield = Free cash flow / Market cap

terms.tooltip: Share of revenue left after the direct cost of goods.
terms.plain_meaning: Of every dollar of sales, how much is left after paying the direct cost of making the product. A 60% gross margin keeps 60 cents to cover everything else and profit.
terms.why_it_matters: It reflects pricing power and production efficiency, and sets the ceiling for overall profitability.
terms.fincompass_use: A profitability ratio from the Statements & ratios desk computed from revenue and cost of goods sold.
terms.limitation: It ignores overhead, marketing, and interest, so a high gross margin can still end in low net profit.
terms.technical_definition: (Revenue − cost of goods sold) divided by revenue.

terms.tooltip: How many times earnings cover interest payments.
terms.plain_meaning: Shows whether a company earns enough to comfortably pay the interest on its debt. A coverage of 5 means operating earnings are five times the interest bill.
terms.why_it_matters: Low coverage warns that debt payments could become hard to meet if earnings dip.
terms.fincompass_use: A solvency ratio from the Statements & ratios desk computed from operating earnings and interest expense.
terms.limitation: It uses accounting earnings, not cash, and a single good year can mask a fragile trend.
terms.technical_definition: EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) divided by interest expense.

terms.tooltip: Value from projected future cash flows discounted to today.
terms.plain_meaning: Discounted cash flow estimates what a business is worth by projecting the cash it will generate in future years and translating those into today's dollars, since money later is worth less than money now.
terms.why_it_matters: It ties a company's value to the cash it actually produces rather than sentiment or price.
terms.fincompass_use: The Valuation desk runs a three-stage DCF and presents a plain-language fair-value gauge, with raw figures behind Research Details. It is a calculator, not a Forecast.
terms.limitation: It is only as good as its assumptions — small changes in growth or discount rate swing the answer widely.
terms.technical_definition: Enterprise value = Σ FCF_t / (1+WACC)^t + terminal value / (1+WACC)^N.

terms.tooltip: Solves for the growth the current price already assumes.
terms.plain_meaning: Flips the usual DCF around: instead of guessing growth to find a value, it takes today's market price and works out what growth rate the market must be assuming to justify it.
terms.why_it_matters: It reframes valuation as a testable question — is the growth baked into the price believable?
terms.fincompass_use: The Valuation desk offers reverse DCF to reveal the market-implied growth behind the current price. A calculator, not a Forecast.
terms.limitation: The implied growth depends on all your other DCF assumptions, so it is a lens, not a verdict.
terms.technical_definition: Solve for the growth rate g such that the DCF value equals the observed market price.
terms.formula: find g such that DCF(g) = current price

terms.tooltip: Blended cost of a company's debt and equity financing.
terms.plain_meaning: The average rate a company pays to fund itself, blending the cost of its debt and the return equity investors demand, weighted by how much of each it uses. It is the discount rate in a DCF.
terms.why_it_matters: It sets the hurdle a company must clear to create value and controls how future cash flows are discounted.
terms.fincompass_use: Used by the Valuation desk as the DCF discount rate; it is a model input you can adjust.
terms.limitation: The cost of equity is itself an estimate, so WACC carries meaningful uncertainty that flows into the DCF.
terms.technical_definition: Weighted average of after-tax cost of debt and cost of equity by their capital weights.

terms.tooltip: The perpetual growth rate assumed after the forecast years.
terms.plain_meaning: After the detailed forecast period, a DCF assumes cash flows grow forever at a slow, steady rate. That rate is the terminal growth, usually kept modest, near long-run economic growth.
terms.why_it_matters: Most of a DCF's value often sits in the terminal period, so this small number carries big weight.
terms.fincompass_use: A DCF input in the Valuation desk that feeds the terminal value calculation.
terms.limitation: Setting it too high quietly inflates the whole valuation; it must stay below the discount rate to be sensible.
terms.technical_definition: The constant perpetual growth rate g applied to cash flows beyond the explicit forecast horizon.

terms.tooltip: Value of all cash flows beyond the explicit forecast years.
terms.plain_meaning: A single lump sum standing in for every cash flow after the detailed forecast ends. Because a business runs indefinitely, this captures the far-future value in one figure.
terms.why_it_matters: It frequently makes up the majority of a DCF's total value, so it dominates the result.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed within the Valuation desk's three-stage DCF from terminal growth and WACC.
terms.limitation: Because it rests on perpetual assumptions, small input changes move it a lot — it is the least certain part of a DCF.
terms.technical_definition: TV = FCF_{N+1} / (WACC − g), the Gordon-growth perpetuity at the end of the forecast horizon.

terms.tooltip: Cash left after running the business and investing in it.
terms.plain_meaning: The cash a company has left after paying to operate and to maintain or grow its assets. It is the money genuinely available to pay down debt, buy back shares, or pay dividends.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the raw material of a DCF and a hard-to-fake sign of financial health.
terms.fincompass_use: The cash-flow input the Valuation desk projects and discounts in the DCF.
terms.limitation: It is lumpy year to year because of capital spending, so one year is a poor guide to normal cash generation.
terms.technical_definition: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditures (FCFF variants also adjust for interest and taxes).

terms.tooltip: Total debt minus cash on hand.
terms.plain_meaning: What a company would still owe if it used all its cash to pay down debt today. Total borrowings minus cash and equivalents. Negative net debt means more cash than debt.
terms.why_it_matters: It bridges enterprise value to equity value and shows true leverage after cash.
terms.fincompass_use: Used by the Valuation desk to convert enterprise value from a DCF into per-share equity value.
terms.limitation: Cash may be trapped overseas or already earmarked, so headline net debt can overstate real flexibility.
terms.technical_definition: Total interest-bearing debt minus cash and cash equivalents.
terms.formula: Net debt = Total debt − Cash & equivalents

terms.tooltip: The growth rate the current price appears to assume.
terms.plain_meaning: The growth in cash flows that would be needed to justify the stock's current price under your DCF assumptions. It tells you what the market seems to be expecting.
terms.why_it_matters: Comparing it to your own view frames whether a stock looks demanding or cheap.
terms.fincompass_use: The headline output of the Valuation desk's reverse DCF.
terms.limitation: It shifts with every other assumption in the model, so treat it as a scenario, not a fact.
terms.technical_definition: The growth rate g that equates the DCF present value to the current market price.

terms.tooltip: Momentum gauge from 0 to 100 flagging overbought/oversold.
terms.plain_meaning: The Relative Strength Index scores recent price momentum from 0 to 100. Readings above 70 are often called overbought and below 30 oversold, hinting a move may be stretched.
terms.why_it_matters: It offers a quick read on whether a recent move looks overextended in either direction.
terms.fincompass_use: A deterministic Technical-indicators calculation shown as context; it does not vote in the Forecast or interpretation policy.
terms.limitation: It can stay overbought or oversold for a long time in a strong trend, giving false reversal signals.
terms.technical_definition: RSI = 100 − 100/(1 + RS), where RS is average gain over average loss across a lookback (typically 14).

terms.tooltip: Trend/momentum from the gap between two moving averages.
terms.plain_meaning: Moving Average Convergence Divergence tracks the difference between a fast and a slow moving average of price, plus a signal line. When the lines cross, it hints momentum may be shifting.
terms.why_it_matters: It is a widely used way to visualize whether momentum is building or fading.
terms.fincompass_use: A deterministic Technical-indicators calculation shown as context; it is not a Forecast feature.
terms.limitation: It lags price because it is built from moving averages and produces whipsaw signals in choppy markets.
terms.technical_definition: MACD = EMA_fast(price) − EMA_slow(price); signal = EMA of MACD (commonly 12, 26, 9).

terms.tooltip: Change in option price per $1 move in the underlying.
terms.plain_meaning: How much an option's price moves when the stock moves one dollar. A delta of 0.5 means the option gains about 50 cents if the stock rises a dollar. It also roughly estimates the odds of finishing in the money.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the primary measure of an option's directional exposure to the stock.
terms.fincompass_use: One of the Greeks the Options desk computes from the Black-Scholes model for a given contract.
terms.limitation: Delta itself changes as the stock moves (that change is gamma), so it is only a local, instantaneous sensitivity.
terms.technical_definition: First derivative of option value with respect to the underlying price: ∂V/∂S.

terms.tooltip: How fast delta changes as the underlying moves.
terms.plain_meaning: The rate at which an option's delta itself changes when the stock moves. High gamma means the directional exposure shifts quickly, so the option's behavior can change fast.
terms.why_it_matters: It warns how unstable an option's directional risk is, especially near the strike close to expiry.
terms.fincompass_use: A Greek computed by the Options desk from the Black-Scholes model.
terms.limitation: It is a second-order effect and, like all Greeks, assumes the model's idealized world holds.
terms.technical_definition: Second derivative of option value with respect to the underlying price: ∂²V/∂S².

terms.tooltip: Change in option price per 1-point change in volatility.
terms.plain_meaning: How much an option's price moves when expected volatility changes by one percentage point. Options gain value when the market expects bigger swings, and vega measures that sensitivity.
terms.why_it_matters: Volatility is a major driver of option prices, so vega captures a big part of the risk.
terms.fincompass_use: A Greek reported by the Options desk from the Black-Scholes model.
terms.limitation: It assumes a single volatility number, whereas real markets show different volatilities across strikes and dates.
terms.technical_definition: First derivative of option value with respect to volatility: ∂V/∂σ.

terms.tooltip: How much value an option loses as one day passes.
terms.plain_meaning: The daily drip of value an option loses simply because time is running out, holding everything else equal. It is the cost of the clock ticking toward expiry.
terms.why_it_matters: Time decay steadily erodes option value, which matters most for option buyers.
terms.fincompass_use: A Greek computed by the Options desk from the Black-Scholes model.
terms.limitation: Decay is not linear — it accelerates near expiry — so a single theta is only a snapshot.
terms.technical_definition: Derivative of option value with respect to time (usually per day): ∂V/∂t.

terms.tooltip: Change in option price per 1-point change in interest rates.
terms.plain_meaning: How much an option's price moves when interest rates change by one percentage point. It is usually the smallest of the Greeks for short-dated options.
terms.why_it_matters: It captures interest-rate sensitivity, which grows for long-dated options.
terms.fincompass_use: A Greek reported by the Options desk from the Black-Scholes model.
terms.limitation: For most short-term options it is minor and easily swamped by moves in price or volatility.
terms.technical_definition: First derivative of option value with respect to the risk-free rate: ∂V/∂r.

terms.tooltip: The volatility the market price of an option implies.
terms.plain_meaning: The amount of future price movement the option's market price is effectively predicting. Rather than measuring past swings, it is backed out of what traders are willing to pay today.
terms.why_it_matters: It reflects the market's forward-looking expectation of turbulence and drives option prices.
terms.fincompass_use: The Options desk can solve for implied volatility from live option chains using Black-Scholes.
terms.limitation: It is model-dependent and varies by strike and expiry (the 'smile'), so a single number oversimplifies.
terms.technical_definition: The volatility input σ that makes the Black-Scholes price equal the observed market price of the option.
terms.formula: σ such that BS(σ) = market price

terms.tooltip: Underlying price at which an option trade makes zero profit.
terms.plain_meaning: The stock price at expiry where an option position exactly recovers its cost — no gain, no loss. Beyond it you profit; short of it you lose the premium.
terms.why_it_matters: It tells you how far the stock must move just for the trade to pay for itself.
terms.fincompass_use: Marked on the Options desk's payoff-at-expiry diagram for a given contract or strategy.
terms.limitation: It only describes the value at expiry and ignores earlier moves, early exercise, and transaction costs.
terms.technical_definition: For a long call: strike + premium paid; for a long put: strike − premium paid (per strategy).
terms.formula: call BE = strike + premium; put BE = strike − premium

terms.tooltip: An option position's profit/loss across ending prices.
terms.plain_meaning: A picture of what an option or strategy is worth at expiration for each possible ending stock price. It shows the shape of your gains and losses at the finish line.
terms.why_it_matters: It makes the risk and reward of an option trade visible at a glance.
terms.fincompass_use: The Options desk draws the payoff-at-expiry diagram as its plain-language first view of a contract or strategy.
terms.limitation: It shows only the expiration snapshot, not the value or risk during the life of the trade.
terms.technical_definition: Position value as a function of underlying price S at expiry, e.g. max(S−K,0) for a long call, minus premium.

terms.tooltip: Classic formula pricing European options.
terms.plain_meaning: A famous formula that estimates a fair price for a European option from the stock price, strike, time left, interest rate, and expected volatility. It underpins most everyday option pricing.
terms.why_it_matters: It provides a consistent, fast benchmark price and the Greeks that describe an option's risks.
terms.fincompass_use: The pricing engine behind the Options desk, used to price contracts, derive Greeks, and back out implied volatility.
terms.limitation: It assumes constant volatility, no early exercise, and lognormal prices — assumptions markets routinely violate.
terms.technical_definition: Closed-form value of a European option: C = S·N(d1) − K·e^(−rT)·N(d2), with d1,d2 functions of S,K,r,σ,T.

terms.tooltip: Total return if a bond is held to maturity.
terms.plain_meaning: The single yearly return you would earn on a bond if you bought it now and held it until it matures, assuming all coupons are reinvested at that same rate. It is the bond market's headline yield.
terms.why_it_matters: It lets you compare bonds with different prices, coupons, and maturities on one number.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Fixed income desk from a bond's price, coupon, and maturity.
terms.limitation: It assumes you hold to maturity and reinvest coupons at the same rate — rarely true in practice.
terms.technical_definition: The discount rate that sets the present value of all coupons and principal equal to the bond's price.

terms.tooltip: Annual coupon as a percentage of the bond's price.
terms.plain_meaning: A simple income measure: the bond's yearly coupon divided by its current price. A $50 coupon on a $1,000 bond is a 5% current yield.
terms.why_it_matters: It gives a quick read on the cash income a bond pays relative to its price.
terms.fincompass_use: A basic yield figure from the Fixed income desk computed from coupon and price.
terms.limitation: It ignores any gain or loss from buying above or below par and the timing of maturity, unlike YTM.
terms.technical_definition: Annual coupon payment divided by the current market price of the bond.

terms.tooltip: Weighted average time to receive a bond's cash flows.
terms.plain_meaning: A measure of a bond's timing, expressed in years: roughly how long, on average, you wait to receive its cash. Longer duration bonds are more sensitive to interest-rate changes.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the core gauge of how much a bond's price will move when rates change.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Fixed income desk (Macaulay duration) as a timing and rate-sensitivity measure.
terms.limitation: As a linear measure it loses accuracy for large rate moves, where convexity matters.
terms.technical_definition: Macaulay duration: present-value-weighted average time to each cash flow, in years.

terms.tooltip: Percent price change per 1-point change in yield.
terms.plain_meaning: Turns duration into a direct price-sensitivity number: roughly the percent a bond's price falls if its yield rises by one percentage point. A modified duration of 7 means about a 7% drop.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the practical link between a rate move and a bond's price move.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported by the Fixed income desk as the standard interest-rate sensitivity measure.
terms.limitation: It is a straight-line approximation that overstates losses and understates gains for big yield moves.
terms.technical_definition: Macaulay duration divided by (1 + yield per period); ≈ −(1/P)(dP/dy).

terms.tooltip: The curvature correction to duration's price estimate.
terms.plain_meaning: Bond prices do not move in a perfectly straight line as yields change — the relationship curves. Convexity measures that curve, refining duration's estimate especially for large rate moves.
terms.why_it_matters: It improves the accuracy of price-change estimates and is generally favorable to bondholders.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Fixed income desk as a second-order complement to duration.
terms.limitation: It is a refinement, not a full model, and standard measures assume cash flows do not change with rates.
terms.technical_definition: Second-order sensitivity of price to yield: (1/P)(d²P/dy²), used to correct the duration estimate.

terms.tooltip: Dollar price change for a 1-basis-point yield move.
terms.plain_meaning: The dollar value of one basis point: how much a bond's price changes in money terms if its yield moves by 0.01%. It expresses rate risk in dollars rather than percent.
terms.why_it_matters: It lets traders size and hedge interest-rate risk in concrete dollar amounts.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported by the Fixed income desk as the dollar sensitivity of a bond to small yield changes.
terms.limitation: Being tied to a tiny move, it is a local estimate and drifts as yields change meaningfully.
terms.technical_definition: Change in bond price for a one-basis-point change in yield: ≈ ModDur × price × 0.0001.

terms.tooltip: Extra yield over a risk-free bond for taking credit risk.
terms.plain_meaning: The additional yield a corporate or risky bond pays above a comparable government bond, compensating investors for the chance the issuer defaults. Wider spreads mean the market sees more risk.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the market's live price of an issuer's credit risk and a barometer of financial stress.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Fixed income desk as the yield difference over a matched Treasury from the live yield curve.
terms.limitation: Spreads also reflect liquidity and market sentiment, not default risk alone.
terms.technical_definition: Yield of a bond minus the yield of a maturity-matched risk-free (Treasury) benchmark.

terms.tooltip: How closely two assets' returns move together, from −1 to 1.
terms.plain_meaning: A number from −1 to 1 describing whether two investments tend to move together. Near 1 they rise and fall together; near −1 they move oppositely; near 0 they are unrelated.
terms.why_it_matters: Low or negative correlations are what make diversification actually reduce risk.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Portfolio desk to build correlation matrices used in risk and diversification analysis.
terms.limitation: Correlations are unstable and tend to spike toward 1 in crises, exactly when diversification is needed most.
terms.technical_definition: Covariance of two return series divided by the product of their standard deviations.

terms.tooltip: How two assets' returns move together, in return units.
terms.plain_meaning: Measures whether two investments tend to move in the same direction, before scaling. Positive means they move together, negative means oppositely, but its size is hard to read directly — which is why correlation is often preferred.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the raw ingredient of portfolio risk math and feeds correlation and risk contributions.
terms.fincompass_use: Used inside the Portfolio desk to assemble the covariance matrix behind portfolio volatility and risk contributions.
terms.limitation: Its unscaled units make it hard to interpret alone, and like correlation it is estimated from unstable history.
terms.technical_definition: Cov(X,Y) = E[(X − μ_X)(Y − μ_Y)], the average product of paired deviations from the mean.

terms.tooltip: How portfolio risk changes if you add a bit more of a holding.
terms.plain_meaning: For each holding, how much the whole portfolio's risk would rise (or fall) if you nudged that position slightly larger. It shows which positions push risk up at the margin.
terms.why_it_matters: It reveals where adding exposure would hurt most, guiding sizing decisions.
terms.fincompass_use: Computed by the Portfolio desk from the covariance matrix and weights as part of risk-contribution analysis.
terms.limitation: It is a local sensitivity based on estimated covariances, so it shifts as weights or correlations change.
terms.technical_definition: The partial derivative of portfolio volatility with respect to an asset's weight: ∂σ_p/∂w_i.

terms.tooltip: Each holding's share of total portfolio risk.
terms.plain_meaning: Splits the portfolio's total risk into slices, one per holding, that add up to the whole. It answers: how much of my overall risk is really coming from each position?
terms.why_it_matters: A small-looking position can be a large risk contributor, and this exposes that hidden concentration.
terms.fincompass_use: Reported by the Portfolio desk as each holding's share of total portfolio volatility.
terms.limitation: It relies on estimated covariances and reflects the current weights, not future behavior.
terms.technical_definition: Weight times marginal contribution: w_i · ∂σ_p/∂w_i; the components sum to total portfolio volatility.

terms.tooltip: Reducing risk by spreading across assets that don't move alike.
terms.plain_meaning: The idea that holding a mix of investments that do not all move together lowers overall risk without necessarily sacrificing return — the one 'free lunch' in investing.
terms.why_it_matters: It is the main lever for cutting risk you are not paid to take.
terms.fincompass_use: Quantified by the Portfolio desk through correlations and risk contributions, showing how much a mix reduces risk.
terms.limitation: Its benefit shrinks just when you need it — correlations rise in crises — and it cannot remove market-wide risk.
terms.technical_definition: The reduction in portfolio volatility below the weighted average of holdings' volatilities due to imperfect correlation.
